chapters.body: Too small to see out of the window, she listened to the beggars in the street below. Teresa Hsu was born in 1898 in Kak Chioh, a village of Swatow, the second of four children. By the time she was five or six, the voices outside told her that people suffered, and she wanted to know why. Her own family was so poor that at times she ate grass. Before light the children rose to fill bamboo baskets with pine needles for fuel in the Swatow hills, then carried laundry in the same baskets to wash in the streams. As she told it decades later, "I may have been a girl of five or six when I heard beggars telling their sad tales along the street."

quote.text: I may have been a girl of five or six when I heard beggars telling their sad tales along the street.

chapters.title: Beggars below the window
chapters.turn: Her mother would show her what to do with empty hands.
chapters.voice: She listened because she was too small to look away.

chapters.body: The pot held the family's whole dinner. Her mother had dug up potatoes and set them to cook when a knock came at the door. A starving beggar stood there with a child. Her mother gave them the entire pot. Teresa's father had left the family for another woman after beating them, and her illiterate mother was raising four children alone. There was nothing left for their own evening meal. Teresa watched the food go out of the door and never forgot it. She kept the lesson for more than a hundred years, that as she later put it, "That was the day I learnt that to give what you have in your hand to others is a great blessing."

quote.text: That was the day I learnt that to give what you have in your hand to others is a great blessing.

chapters.title: The pot of potatoes
chapters.turn: A boat to Penang would lead her to a classroom door.
chapters.voice: An empty pot taught her more than a full one ever could.

chapters.body: She swept the convent corridors each morning before the lessons began. When the last uncle who supported them left, the family had sold their lace to pay for a boat passage to Penang, and Teresa arrived with her grandmother, her mother and her three siblings. In Penang she and her mother worked as cleaners at a Catholic convent. Unschooled at 27, she persuaded the nuns in 1925 to let her sit in on the children's classes. She studied from books the nuns had found for her, for as she remembered, "The nuns got us free books from rich former pupils." About three and a half years later she passed the Senior Cambridge examination.

quote.text: The nuns got us free books from rich former pupils.

chapters.title: Sweeping for lessons
chapters.turn: Reading would take her much farther than Penang.
chapters.voice: A cleaner at the back of the class learned to read.

chapters.body: By lamplight she copied shorthand strokes into an exercise book. Teresa had left Penang for Hong Kong in 1933, cleaning by day and learning English, shorthand and typing by night until she was hired as a stenographer. In 1939 she moved to Chongqing as secretary and bookkeeper at a German news agency. When the city became unsafe, she gave up the well-paid job and volunteered with the Friends' Ambulance Unit. She faced the dying and saw that no one there knew how to save them. She decided her vocation was to nurse the sick and destitute, for as she later explained, "The poor can at least beg, but the others, you either go to them, or they die."

quote.text: The poor can at least beg, but the others, you either go to them, or they die.

chapters.title: Shorthand by night
chapters.turn: In that work she met someone she would not forget.
chapters.voice: She traded a salary for a way to help.

chapters.body: He danced the foxtrot and made the whole room laugh. In the ambulance service Teresa met Brian Sorenson, a 24-year-old blond, blue-eyed volunteer. She said it was the only time she came close to having her own family. About three years later, after she had left for London, he boarded a plane to join her and was killed when it crashed. She spoke of him half a century later without bitterness, remembering only the brightness. She kept his memory beside her work. As she recalled, "He was so cheerful—and so good at dancing the foxtrot." She never married.

quote.text: He was so cheerful—and so good at dancing the foxtrot.

chapters.title: The foxtrot
chapters.turn: A hungry stranger waited at a Shanghai hotel gate.
chapters.voice: For once she imagined a family of her own.

chapters.body: At the gate of the grand Shanghai hotel a starving man asked her for a few cents. Teresa had just finished a meal inside with British friends in 1945. She went home and threw out her lipstick, her rouge and her nail polish. She kept nothing for display after that. The meeting at the gate stayed with her as the point when her life narrowed to one purpose. As she later described it, "I'll never touch a cent that belongs to the poor person. That was the start. After that, I was free."

quote.text: I'll never touch a cent that belongs to the poor person. That was the start. After that, I was free.

chapters.title: Lipstick in the bin
chapters.turn: She was 47 and needed a new skill.
chapters.voice: She left vanity at the hotel gate.

chapters.body: She was 47 and asking for a place meant for the young. Far past the age limit, Teresa wrote to the Nursing Council in London in 1945, and the matron replied that they were touched and would train her. She had told them, "I'm grossly overaged, but for me, it's a dedication, not a livelihood." She trained without fees at the Royal Free Hospital in London. She remained eight years in England. She nursed in hospitals and she travelled across Europe with the International Voluntary Service for Peace, taking work where help was needed.

quote.text: I'm grossly overaged, but for me, it's a dedication, not a livelihood.

chapters.title: Grossly overaged
chapters.turn: A river and a letter would call her away.
chapters.voice: Too old for school, she went to school.

chapters.body: She watched fish playing in a river and decided she would eat no more living things. Teresa had sailed to Paraguay in 1953 with the Bruderhof, the Society of Brothers, and stayed eight years, often the only trained nurse and midwife at a small hospital. While there she became a conscious vegetarian. A letter from home then called her back to her ageing mother in Penang. Her mother told her, as Teresa repeated all her life, "Poor people you get everywhere, but you have only one mother." She returned to Penang to be with her mother. She had forgiven her father.

quote.text: Poor people you get everywhere, but you have only one mother.

chapters.title: Only one mother
chapters.turn: Singapore would give her work for decades.
chapters.voice: Duty pulled her home across an ocean.

chapters.body: The bungalow at Jalan Payoh Lai stood on 0.6 hectares of land. In 1963 Teresa had become the unsalaried matron of Kwong Wai Shiu Hospital in Singapore. With her elder sister Ursula, principal of CHIJ Bukit Timah, who paid for it, she opened the Home for the Aged Sick in 1965, one of Singapore's first homes for the elderly sick. Ursula bought the plot with its bungalow, and Teresa always credited her, saying, "My sister supported me, she was the one who bought this land for me." The beds filled almost at once.

quote.text: My sister supported me, she was the one who bought this land for me.

chapters.title: The matron without a salary
chapters.turn: Fruit trees would have to pay for medicine.
chapters.voice: Two sisters built a home for strangers.

chapters.body: Ten coconut trees and a dozen banana trees grew behind the bungalow. Teresa sold their fruit to help buy medicine after she and Ursula turned the bungalow and servants' quarters into wards. Ursula paid from her salary while Teresa ran the home. By 1970 there were about 100 patients and no money to cope, so they handed the deeds to the Society for the Aged Sick, formed by Rotary Club members, which built three blocks. She stayed on as matron. Ursula died in 1973 and left Teresa a small fortune. She used it to buy flats for people with nowhere to go, five in Singapore and two in Malaysia. Within a few years Lucy and Anthony died within weeks of each other, leaving her without family.
chapters.title: Ten coconut trees
chapters.turn: Retirement would not slow her rounds.
chapters.voice: She turned fruit into shelter for a hundred people.

chapters.body: After she retired as the home's matron in the early 1980s, she moved into a small flat attached to it. Each month she climbed out of a volunteer's car with bags of rice, sugar and biscuits and envelopes holding S$20 to S$180 for elderly people on public assistance. With co-worker Sharana Rao and volunteer drivers she ran Heart to Heart Service, the new name for her old Friends of the Poor. Outside her flat an orange plant someone had thrown away carried her handwritten tag with its date of rebirth, as she told visitors, "A live thing should never be left alone to die." A visitor found her barefoot in a spotless flat she cleaned herself.

quote.text: A live thing should never be left alone to die.

chapters.title: Heart to Heart
chapters.turn: At 110 she still sang for her guests.
chapters.voice: No one was too small to be carried home.

chapters.body: She stood before about 200 people in Penang and made them laugh. At 112 Teresa still rose at 4 am for yoga, which she had taken up at 69 after buying a book called Forever Young, Forever Healthy, and later taught at temples, hospitals and schools. At 110 she had sung visitors a German song and a Cantonese nursery rhyme and read without glasses. Asked in Penang whether she had ever been ill, as she told them, "The sick demons forgot to visit me." On Wednesday 7 December 2011 she died peacefully at home, aged 113. By her instruction she was cremated the same day, with no rituals or announcement, and no one claimed her ashes.

quote.text: The sick demons forgot to visit me.

chapters.title: The sick demons forgot
chapters.turn: She left nothing behind but full plates.
chapters.voice: She laughed at illness and shared everything else.

conflicts.choice: The book uses 1898, the corroborated date, and notes it was never independently verified.
The book gives no age or year for the move to Penang and follows the 1925 dating for schooling.
conflicts.topic: Age and year of the move to Penang

conflicts.choice: The book leaves out the arranged-marriage escape rather than fixing it to a year.
The book follows 1939 for the move to Chongqing.
The book follows 1945, aged 47, for writing to London.
The book follows 1963 for becoming matron in Singapore.
The book says early 1980s for retirement and gives no single year.
The book leaves out the claim she set up Assunta Hospital with Anthony and says only she returned to Penang.
The book keeps only that she had forgiven her father and omits when and where she nursed him.
The book follows Friends of the Poor renamed Heart to Heart Service around 1983.
